strengths: Extensive and well-designed empirical study: results are reported on two major benchmarks (SUPERB, HEAR) plus downstream fine-tuning (ASR, AudioSet tagging), across three model scales (94M/327M/600M) and both single- and dual-domain settings, giving a fairly complete picture of the method's behavior.

The core idea—using multi-codebook vector quantization (MVQ) of teacher SSL representations to produce fine-grained discrete targets for masked prediction—is a sensible and, to my knowledge, novel bridge between the token-prediction paradigm popular in speech SSL and the more irregular acoustic structure of general audio, addressing a genuine gap (domain-specific SSL objectives).

Strong quantitative results: the speech-only SPEAR model matches or beats WavLM Large on 12/15 SUPERB tasks under matched data/model size, and the dual-domain model narrows the gap to single-domain specialists while outperforming a similarly-scoped concurrent unified model (USAD) on both SUPERB and HEAR.

Thorough ablation studies (Appendix G) examining teacher choice, α weighting of masked/unmasked loss, number of codebooks, dual-domain loss balancing strategies, and a qualitative UMAP analysis showing MVQ preserves speaker identity far better than k-means — these add genuine mechanistic insight beyond simple benchmark numbers.

Honest reporting of limitations and negative results (e.g., VC degradation with scale, weaker HEAR scores vs. much larger Dasheng 1.2B, imbalanced data mixture hurting audio-side unification), which strengthens the credibility of the empirical claims.
weaknesses: The method is essentially knowledge distillation from strong existing domain-specific teacher models (WavLM Large, Dasheng 1.2B) reframed as an 'SSL' objective; the student's ceiling is shown in the teacher-selection ablation (G.1) to be closely tied to teacher quality, which somewhat undercuts the framing of SPEAR as an independent, generalizable SSL recipe rather than a compression/distillation pipeline contingent on pre-existing strong single-domain models.

The core technical novelty is limited: MVQ itself is taken directly from prior work (Guo et al., 2023), and the masked-token-prediction objective is a well-established SSL recipe (HuBERT-style); the contribution is mainly the combination and application to a dual-domain setting rather than a fundamentally new method.

Evidence for genuine 'unification' is mixed: the dual-domain model shows slight degradations on several SUPERB understanding/paralinguistic tasks relative to the speech-only variant, and on HEAR the unified XLarge model trails the (much larger, more data-rich) Dasheng 1.2B on environment and music tasks; the claimed synergy is real but modest and partly obscured by an acknowledged imbalanced data mixture (87% speech).

No code or checkpoints are available at submission time (deferred to post-review), which limits independent verification of the many benchmark numbers despite otherwise good documentation of hyperparameters.

Some comparisons across tables mix different pre-training data scales and model sizes (e.g., Dasheng-Base with 20x more data, WavLM Large vs. differently-sized SPEAR variants), which, while transparently disclosed, makes some 'state-of-the-art' claims less clean and requires careful reading to properly contextualize.

strengths: Proposes a genuinely novel and well-motivated unification of speech and audio SSL via fine-grained multi-codebook vector quantisation (MVQ) tokens, addressing a real limitation of coarse k-means-based token prediction in the audio domain.

Very extensive empirical validation across two major benchmarks (SUPERB and HEAR) plus downstream fine-tuning on ASR and audio tagging, at three model scales (Base/Large/XLarge up to 600M params), providing strong evidence for the claims.
Speech-domain model matches or exceeds the strong WavLM Large baseline on 12/15 SUPERB tasks under a matched-data, matched-size comparison, which is a rigorous and convincing head-to-head result.

Thorough and informative ablation studies (Appendix G) covering teacher model choice, masked/unmasked loss weighting, number of codebooks, dual-domain training strategy, and a qualitative UMAP analysis showing MVQ tokens retain speaker information that k-means discards — these ablations meaningfully deepen understanding of why the method works.
The asymmetrical dual-domain loss design is empirically justified via a 3-way comparison (JOINT/DISJOINT/ASYMMETRICAL), showing it is not an arbitrary design choice.
Good transparency about limitations (e.g., VC underperformance, imbalanced audio data causing HEAR gaps vs Dasheng 1.2B) rather than hiding weak results.
Reproducibility statement with commitment to release code and checkpoints, plus detailed hyperparameter tables in the appendix.
weaknesses: The framework fundamentally relies on strong pre-existing teacher models (WavLM Large, Dasheng 1.2B) to generate MVQ targets, making the approach closer to a distillation-plus-SSL-objective hybrid; while the paper argues the students can surpass their teachers on individual metrics, overall representation quality (e.g., on HEAR speech/music categories) still lags behind the larger, more heavily-trained Dasheng 1.2B teacher, suggesting the framework's ceiling is still influenced by teacher/data quality.

General audio pre-training data (13k hours) is substantially smaller and less diverse than speech data (84k-197k hours), leading to a persistent imbalance that shows up as degraded performance on some audio/music tasks for the dual-domain models relative to single-domain audio models — a limitation the authors acknowledge but do not resolve.

The 'first unified SSL framework' framing is somewhat strong given related prior work (Gong et al. 2022, USAD/Chang et al. 2025) already explores joint speech+audio pretraining; while the paper differentiates its objective (mask-token-prediction SSL loss vs. feature-matching KD), the novelty framing could be tempered.

Results on some SUPERB tasks (ST, QbE, VC) and the VC generation task specifically show the dual/single-domain SPEAR models underperforming baselines or degrading with scale, which is not fully explained beyond a brief hypothesis about overfitting.

The additional training complexity and computational overhead of training separate MVQ quantisers per teacher domain, plus maintaining two frozen large teacher models during pre-training, is not discussed in terms of resource cost, which is relevant for reproducibility/practical adoption.

The λ hyperparameter (weighting the audio-specific loss in dual-domain training) appears fixed at 0.1 without an ablation showing sensitivity, despite this being a potentially important balance parameter.
